pl-l4d5c3-d1e115.summary: Asks what the power of baptism is that Christ kept for himself and could have given to servants.

pl-l4d5c3-d1e118.summary: Reports the common view that it is the power of forgiving sins in baptism.
claims: Many identify the power of baptism with the power to forgive sins.

pl-l4d5c3-d1e121.summary: Reports an objection: the power of forgiving sins in God is God, so he could not give it to any servant, since he could not make anyone be what he is or have his essence, for whom to be is to be able. If he could give it, he could also give the power to create, which is no greater.
claims: God's power to forgive is his essence and cannot be given.
Giving the power to forgive would imply giving the power to create.

pl-l4d5c3-d1e125.summary: Replies that God could have given not the same power by which he is powerful, but a created power by which a servant could forgive sins as minister, not author, yet not without God as author: as he sanctifies outwardly in ministry, he would cleanse inwardly, God using his word as a ministry. So God could create through someone as minister, working with and in him, as in our good works he works and we work, he with us and in us, we as his ministers, not authors. So he could give the servant power to forgive in baptism, the Lord working with and in the servant; the Lord sanctifies by invisible grace, the servant by the visible sacrament.
claims: God could give a created, ministerial power to forgive sins.
God could create through a creature as minister.
In good works God works with and in us as his ministers.
The Lord sanctifies by grace, the servant by the sacrament.

pl-l4d5c3-d1e128.summary: Quotes Augustine on Leviticus: the Lord says 'I am the Lord who sanctifies', and it is said to Moses 'you shall sanctify him'. Moses sanctifies by visible sacraments through ministry; the Lord by invisible grace through the Spirit, in which lies the whole fruit of the visible sacraments, which profit nothing without it.
claims: The minister sanctifies by visible sacraments, God by invisible grace.
Visible sacraments profit nothing without invisible grace.

pl-l4d5c3-d1e137.summary: Concludes modestly: if anyone can explain this better, he does not begrudge it.

pl-l4d5c3.summary: Asks what the power of baptism is that Christ kept and could have given. Many say it is the power of forgiving sins in baptism. Others object that this power in God is God, which he could not give to a creature, and that if he could give it he could give the power to create. Lombard replies that he could give not the very power by which he is powerful, but a created power by which a servant could forgive sins as minister, not author, with God as author working with and in him, as the minister sanctifies outwardly; likewise God could create through someone as minister, as he works with and in us in our good works. So the Lord sanctifies by invisible grace, the servant by the visible sacrament, as Augustine says of Moses. Lombard ends modestly: if anyone can explain this better, he does not begrudge it.
claims: Some identify the power of baptism with the power to forgive sins.
God could not give his own power, which is God, to a creature.
God could give a created power to forgive sins ministerially.
God could create through a creature as minister, not author.
God sanctifies by invisible grace, the minister by the visible sacrament.
